segments.narration: Three schoolgirls started laughing and couldn't stop for days. Kashasha, Tanganyika, the thirtieth of January, nineteen sixty-two.
It spread. Ninety-five of the school's one hundred fifty-nine pupils were affected, in fits that ran from hours to sixteen days.
Doctors found nothing. No fever, no toxin, no poisoned food. So what travels through a school and leaves no trace in the blood?
The school closed in March. The laughter went home with the girls, reached Nshamba village, and eventually touched about a thousand people across fourteen schools.
Medical officers Rankin and Philip published the answer in nineteen sixty-three: mass psychogenic illness. Real symptoms, no pathogen, stress moving through a community like weather.

verdicts.claim: The outbreak began on 30 January 1962 at a mission-run girls' boarding school in Kashasha, Tanganyika, starting with three pupils.
verdicts.note: 92% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: 95 of the school's 159 pupils were affected, with symptoms lasting from a few hours to 16 days.
verdicts.note: 88% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 3 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Investigating medical officers found no infectious or toxic cause for the episodes.
verdicts.note: Rankin and Philip's investigation found no organic cause and settled on mass psychogenic illness; the reported symptoms were respiratory spasms, restlessness and pain rather than signs of infection.

verdicts.claim: The school closed in March 1962, the outbreak reached Nshamba village and other communities, and about 1,000 people were affected across 14 closed schools.
verdicts.note: 71% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 3 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Medical officers A. M. Rankin and P. J. Philip published their investigation in the Central African Journal of Medicine in 1963, diagnosing mass psychogenic illness.
verdicts.note: Rankin and Philip published in the Central African Journal of Medicine in May 1963; mass psychogenic illness remains the accepted explanation.
